(2020) Coal gasification and natural gas reforming are considered highly mature fossil-based production processes that have a high level of deployment around the world. CCS technology is less mature, with only 50 CCS facilities operating around the world, capturing 51 MMT/yr of CO as of 2024 2 (Global CCS Institute 2024). CCS cost reductions through technology learning would be expected as the number of low-pollution fossil-based hydrogen production facilities and other CCS-equipped facilities grow over time. Commercially available electricity-based hydrogen production technologies include PEM, alkaline, and solid oxide electrolyzers. Each type of electrolyzer operates on electricity, which is used to split water fed to the electrolyzer into hydrogen and oxygen (H O + electricity  H + 2 2 46 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. ½O ). Hydrogen produced via electrolysis using renewable electricity (e.g., from solar panels or 2 wind turbines) is commonly referred to as green hydrogen. Of the electrolyzer technologies, alkaline is the most mature, operating since the early 1900s in response to growing hydrogen demand for ammonia production. It was not until the 1980s when low-cost hydrogen from SMR began to outpace alkaline electrolyzer hydrogen production (Krishnan et al. 2020). Traditional alkaline electrolyzers typically operated at a constant output with limited ramping capabilities, but more recent alkaline electrolyzer technology may have the ability to operate directly using electricity generated from intermittent renewables (Cockerill 2020; Ehlers et al. 2023). If so, this would be a cheaper alternative to PEM electrolyzers, which are notable for their ability to ramp with renewable electricity generated from wind and solar such that the hydrogen production is renewable. The higher cost for PEM electrolyzers compared to alkaline can be attributed to the lower maturity of the technology and expensive rare materials, such as iridium, that are used in the electrode catalyst (DOE 2023b; Badgett et al. 2024). Unlike PEM and alkaline electrolyzers, which both operate at low temperature, solid oxide electrolyzers require heat as an input, allowing this type of electrolyzer to achieve higher electrical conversion efficiency. Therefore, solid oxide electrolyzers are most suitable at facilities that already generate excess heat, such as a nuclear power plant. Instead of being lost to the environment, heat is diverted to the electrolyzer to boost process efficiency.
